accroche: A two-line poem slipped into a 1902 treatise still explains today why other people's gaze shapes the idea we have of ourselves
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1902, the American sociologist Charles Horton Cooley, then teaching at the University of Michigan, publishes *Human Nature and the Social Order*. In the middle of a chapter on what he calls the “social self,” he slips in two lines borrowed from a poem: “Each to each a mirror, reflecting the other who passes.” The image is beautiful, but misleading if taken literally: a mirror does not judge what it reflects, whereas it is precisely the supposed judgment of others that, according to Cooley, shapes the idea we have of ourselves.

## Three Elements, Not a Reflection

Cooley calls this mechanism the “looking-glass self,” and distinguishes three elements in it: the imagination of our appearance to another person, the imagination of the judgment that person passes on this appearance, and a resulting self-feeling, such as pride or shame. He insists on the second element, the one that the comparison with a mirror does not suggest by itself: “what moves us to pride or shame is not the mere mechanical reflection of ourselves, but a sentiment imputed to the other, the imagined effect of this reflection on his mind.” Feeling ashamed before a person we regard as upright, or cowardly before someone brave, therefore does not depend on what that person actually thinks. It depends on what we imagine they think, whether that image is accurate or not.

## A Century Later, a Test

Cooley's thesis remains, for the most part, an introspective observation, with no data to back it. In 2003, the sociologists King-To Yeung and John Levi Martin put it to an empirical test, using network data collected in fifty-six communities. Their results confirm part of the mechanism: individuals do incorporate, into the idea they have of themselves, the perceived judgment of people who occupy a higher social position than their own. But the study, conducted over time, also reveals a reverse movement that Cooley had not foreseen: through constant actions, a person can gradually change the judgment others hold of them, rather than simply adjusting to it. The mirror, in short, does not merely return an image: in the long run, it sometimes happens that we redraw it.

citation.texte: A self-idea of this kind seems to have three principal elements: the imagination of our appearance to the other person, the imagination of his judgment of that appearance, and a sort of self-feeling, such as pride or mortification.
citation.source: Human Nature and the Social Order, Charles Scribner's Sons, 1902, ch. 5 “The Social Self,” p. 152

carte.punch: “Each to each a mirror”: a poem slipped into a 1902 book on the gaze of others
carte.idee: In 1902, Cooley describes the “looking-glass self”: the idea we have of ourselves depends less on others' actual gaze than on the judgment we imagine in them. A century later, a study of fifty-six communities confirms the mechanism, and shows that it also works the other way around.

quiz.question: According to Cooley, what shapes the feeling of pride or shame in the “looking-glass self”?
choix: The actual judgment that others express publicly out loud
The judgment we imagine the other holds of our appearance, whether accurate or not
The mere fact of being observed, independent of any idea of judgment
The social position of the person looking at us, whatever their judgment
quiz.explication: It is neither the judgment actually expressed, nor mere observation, nor the other's social position alone that produces self-feeling: Cooley insists that it is the judgment we imagine in the other, accurate or not, that provokes pride or shame, which the comparison with a mechanical mirror does not suggest by itself.

choix: At Columbia University, in New York

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Yeung and Martin's empirical test in 2003 reveal that Cooley had not foreseen?
choix: That the looking-glass self mechanism works only in children
That a person can, through constant actions, change the judgment of others
That others' judgment has no measurable effect on self-feeling
That the looking-glass self is observed only in nonindustrialized societies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study, conducted over time in fifty-six communities, reveals a reverse movement that Cooley had not foreseen: through constant actions, a person can change others' judgment of them.

Network data collected in fifty-six communities
Opinion polls conducted in ten different countries
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 2003, Yeung and Martin put Cooley's thesis to an empirical test using network data collected in fifty-six communities, whereas Cooley had offered only an introspective observation.
